fixes.explanation: Close, friend, but the poem goes the other way. It says, "The heart of her husband trusts in her…" (Proverbs 31:11). A worried heart paces the kitchen and checks the oven every two minutes. The word in the verse is trust.

That's right, friend. The poem says, "The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value." (Proverbs 31:11). Trust is the word, not worry. Nothing in the verse says his heart is worried.
You've got it, baker. The poem says her husband "…lacks nothing of value." (Proverbs 31:11). Not one thing of value is on his lacking list. That's the whole verse in one breath.
A little money is a fair guess, baker, but the verse doesn't name money. It says her husband "…lacks nothing of value." (Proverbs 31:11). The word is "nothing," and it's about things of value.

A storehouse is a sensible idea, baker, but the poem doesn't say it. It says, "…from her earnings she plants a vineyard." (Proverbs 31:16). Planting a vineyard is what her earnings go toward. No building is mentioned.
A well is a good thing to dig, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The poem says, "…from her earnings she plants a vineyard." (Proverbs 31:16). Planting a vineyard is what her earnings go toward.

You'd think so, friend. After a field and a vineyard, I'd be flat on the counter with flour in my eyebrows. But the poem says, "She girds herself with strength and shows that her arms are strong." (Proverbs 31:17). Strong arms is what the verse says about her.
That's it, baker. The poem says, "She opens her arms to the poor…" (Proverbs 31:20). Her hands work the spindle, and her arms open to the poor. That's a lot of arm work.

Nobles are an easy guess, baker, since this is a poem about noble character. But the verse says, "She opens her arms to the poor…" (Proverbs 31:20). The poor are the ones it names. Nobles aren't mentioned in that verse.

Right, baker. The poem says, "When it snows, she has no fear for her household, for they are all clothed in scarlet." (Proverbs 31:21). Snow comes, and she has no fear for her household. The reason given is that they're all clothed in scarlet.

Firewood sounds smart, baker, but the poem doesn't say it. It says she has no fear for her household "…for they are all clothed in scarlet." (Proverbs 31:21). The reason given is clothing. Everyone in the household is wearing it.

You've got it, baker. The poem says, "Her husband is known at the city gates, where he sits among the elders of the land." (Proverbs 31:23). So he's known at the gates, sitting among the elders. That's the spot the verse names.

That's it, baker. The poem says, "She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue." (Proverbs 31:26). When she speaks, wisdom comes out. I wish my mouth worked that way before I'd had a chance to wake up.

It's the other way around, friend. The poem says, "She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness." (Proverbs 31:27). So the poem says she does not eat the bread of idleness. She watches over the affairs of her household instead.

That's right, friend. The poem says she "…watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness." (Proverbs 31:27). She keeps an eye on the affairs of her household. The bread of idleness isn't hers to eat.
You've got it, baker. The poem says, "Her children rise up and call her blessed…" (Proverbs 31:28). They rise up and call her blessed. That's about the best applause a person can get.

That's right, baker. The poem says, "Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised." (Proverbs 31:30). The poem puts charm and beauty on one side, and the woman who fears the LORD on the other. She's the one it says to praise.

You've got it, baker. The poem ends, "Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates." (Proverbs 31:31). Her works are the ones praising her, and the place is the gates. Nothing else is named as the one praising.
